articleTitle: The electric talking machine: Electric motors were first used to drive early phonographs in the late 1880s
Computer displays: New choices, new tradeoffs: Advances on several fronts let users and designers juggle lightness, brightness, and price as well as much-sought-after flatness
abstract: The most powerful computer in the world is of no use to anyone unless it can communicate the results of its calculations. Throughout the 1950s and 1960s, and on into the 1970s, most computers clattered out information for users on machines that were derivatives of the teletype, and many of the habits of computing born then still exist today. Since then, however, so-called soft-copy displays have become more and more prevalent, most of them in the form of cathode-ray-tube (CRT) displays - monitor screens that resemble television screens.

articleTitle: The DIP may take its final bows: The dual-in-line package, the reigning IC package for several generations, is losing position to newcomers for packaging advanced chips
abstract: The DIP is a has-been. A star of the semiconductor industry for 20 years, the dual-in-line package is being upstaged by a raft of new packages with labels like “small outline,” “chip carrier,” and “pin-grid array.”

The first lightweight plastic bullet exploded out of the muzzle at a blistering 2 kilometers per second, lodging itself in a bullet trap across the room. The fifth projectile, shot split-seconds later, never made it out of the barrel.

articleTitle: Microprocessors: New 32-bit microprocessors in CMOS perform virtual-memory functions on the chip and show promise in applications ranging from multiprocessing to fault-tolerant computing
abstract: For the growing class of 32-bit microprocessors, developments last year favored implementation in CMOS, integration of support functions such as cache memory and memory management on the chip, and execution of instructions at a rate well over 1 million per second.

articleTitle: Satellites and mobile phones: Planning a marriage: Dramatic improvements in rural communications may be in the offing as direct service by satellite to mobile phones moves closer to reality
abstract: You are part of a geological exploration team working in a remote area of Wyoming, and you have encountered a problem that you cannot solve by yourself. With a portable telephone unit, you try to reach a colleague in your company's Chicago branch. She is not in her office, but with a second call you reach her directly as she is driving east on Interstate 80 in western Pennsylvania. Through your telephone conversation, the two of you resolve the problem quickly and your work can then proceed.

articleTitle: Communications: Highlights include the AT&T divestiture, a new long-distance record in fiber-optic communications, local-area networks, and cellular radio
abstract: The boundary lines between telephone and data communications blurred further last year, mainly because of the breakup of the American Telephone & Telegraph Co. in the United States, which became effective Jan. 1, 1984. With AT&T's divestiture of its regional companies offering local telephone service, AT&T became legally free to diversify into areas of technology that had previously been ruled off-limits. Exercising that new freedom right away, the company in the summer announced its first personal computer, the AT&T 6300 [see "Personal computers," page 45].
A rising tide of skepticism about the viability of the four-year engineering curriculum is evident.

articleTitle: Research and development: Xerox palo alto research center(PARC)
abstract: The director of the Xerox Palo Alto Research Center shows how his management philosophy worked in launching the center and making it a success. The three principles followed by the director were to: (1) recruit the best, most creative researchers; (2) give the researchers the most supportive environment, including ample amounts of the most advanced instrumentation; and (3) work the business needs of the corporation into the program through selective budgetary preferences. The way in which the director recruited, organized the research, and selected the technologies is recounted.

articleTitle: Robots in the home: Promises, promises: While great expectations are held for certain robot types, the robots for fun and educational purposes are limited in their adaptability to useful tasks
abstract: True or false: home robots can bring in the Wall Street Journal, guard your home against intruders, vacuum the carpets, serve canapes to guests at a cocktail party, help with the dishes afterward, and be a friend and companion whose society and help you can enjoy in a health club or in Booth One at Chicago's Pump Room.

articleTitle: Charles H. House on instrumentation: A marriage of computers and test equipment
abstract: Electronics is at a watershed in terms of both useful performance and impact upon society. As a consequence, the design process for electronic products is undergoing substantial revision. This revision is exciting, even awesome, in its implication for productivity. And the implications for test instrumentation " in terms of quality of product design, merged synthesis-analysis requirement, and reliability and supportability of the delivered product " are profound. Indeed the ultimate use of much of the new electronics capability will be in "instrumentation for society."

articleTitle: Minis and mainframes: Superminicomputers push mainframe performance, mainframes operate at supercomputer speeds, and supercomputers reach 400 million operations per second
abstract: Bigger, faster, more powerful - those have been the acknowledged trends in computing for some time, and 1984 was no exception. Probably the most clear-cut development was in the area of superminicomputers, where the typical performance of a top-end machine increased from a little more than 1 million instructions per second to between 4 and 5 million. The most powerful new machines overlap the bottom and middle of the mainframe performance range.

Enhanced by advances in microelectronics, the use of burglar-alarm systems for the home is on the rise in the United States. Home owners in suburbia and apartment dwellers in big cities are among the big users of burglar-alarm systems, and with electronic intelligence and control now offered at reasonable cost, other protective measures - like fire detection and “panic buttons” to summon medical help - have been added.

A telephone call probably saved the life of Jessica, the nine-week-old daughter of Warren Graham, an electrician in Alexandria, Va. The call woke Graham, who had fallen asleep in a chair in Jessica's room. Startled, he saw that her face had turned blue - she was no longer breathing. He revived her with mouth-to-mouth resuscitation, saving her from sudden-infant-death syndrome, which takes the lives of 7000 babies each year throughout the United States.

articleTitle: Karmarkar's algorithm: A threat to simplex? An elegant new method of solving linear equations has yet to be thoroughly tested
abstract: For almost 40 years, linear programming has been a stable discipline, marked by incremental improvements to the established standard algorithm, the “simplex method.” But in the summer of 1984, Narendra Karmarkar, a 30-year-old mathematician at AT&T Bell Laboratories, described an elegant and perhaps revolutionary new algorithm for solving linear programming problems, which he claimed was far faster than the simplex method.

articleTitle: John D. Musa on software: Productivity, quality, and human factors
abstract: As the software area continues to evolve rapidly, one thing is clear: computer programs are not what they used to be. Initially software was designed for standard repetitive problems such as the processing and issuing of insurance policies. Now, however, software increasingly deals with adaptive problem solving through interaction with a professional or other specialist. This interactive handling of functions has sparked growing interest in artificial intelligence and knowledge-based systems. These systems have some problem-solving capability tied to an organized base of knowledge.

Six experts were invited to provide overviews of fundamental areas of electrotechnology for this annual state-of-the-art review. In addition, inputs for the other Erticles were obtained from some 75 contributors; many of the contributions were solicited from !eaders within the IEEE's technical societies by issue coordinator Ronald Jurgen. All the specialists were asked to focus on near-term developments and to limit their blue-sky projections. They were also asked to cite specific manufacturers and equipment models where possible, to exemplify important technical developments. The six experts and their topics are: Eric Aupperle, computes; John Musa, software; Paul Green, communications; Bernard Murphy, solid state; Charles House, instrumentation; and John Dougherty, power and energy.

articleTitle: Industrial electronics: Robots, vision systems, smart sensors, adaptive controls, and an automation protocol accelerate integrated manufacturing
abstract: At the General Electric Co.'s aircraft-engine plant in Evendale, Ohio, a developmental “seeing” robot-welder joins the curved edges of two steel plates, continuously adjusting the track of the torch, the amount of electric-arc current, and the welding-wire feed rate to ensure a high-quality, even seam. The device welds 1.5- or 3-millimeter-thick plates at rates up to 15 centimeters per minute, or twice the average speed of a human welder.

They look like giant lips, baseball bats, or cartoon characters. They remember phone numbers when you can't. They screen your phone calls, or tell you someone is breaking into your house. They respond to your verbal commands, they question the identity of callers or give them your forwarding number. They turn on your air conditioner or lights, or turn them off. They let you talk to your wife in the kitchen or your grandmother 3000 miles away.

The high-tech house offers relief from summer heat not only by means of power-hungry air conditioners, but also through shade trees placed along the south side of the building. Heat in winter can come from a gas-fired furnace and also from warm air radiated from a solar mass beneath the floor. Smarter design and new technology are keeping the options open.

articleTitle: Impact 2000: A place in the sun: Sponsored by Boston Edison as an energy-conservation experiment, this home in the suburbs was seen during its construction by public-television viewers across the United States
abstract: It is a house with a roof that generates electricity, a heating system that extracts heat from 400 feet below the ground, walls that store heat during the day and release it at night, windows that allow more heat to enter than escape, and fireplaces that draw combustion air from the outside. It is called Impact 2000, and money was no object in building it in Brookline, Mass. The house will be put up for sale next month at current market value, which is estimated to be $500 000.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: Don't hang up yet
abstract: It was not our intention to make this a special issue on divestiture. When we began our planning we promised ourselves it would not center on the separation of the Bell operating companies from AT&T. That subject, we believed, had been thoroughly covered by the press in general - from the dailies to the newsweeklies to the business press. Television had even done its share, and books had already been published by “insiders.” Our intent was to probe into the postdivestiture future of telecommunications. The assignments we doled out among ourselves reflected that intent. Nevertheless, as each editor began preliminary research, it became clear that to look ahead with intelligence meant that to study the past was a necessity. And so divestiture and deregulation became an integral part of the report.

The plain television set is not so plain anymore; it has been undergoing subtle change and taking on new functions. Television and top-quality audio are merging into an audiovisual entertainment center in the home, and at the heart of the new setup is either the television set or a monitor - a high-quality cathode-ray tube with supporting electronics but no tuner or speakers.

We are all idiosyncratic and never more so than at the end of the day, when we are alone, when we unwind, when we prepare for confronting in dreams what we prefer to ignore during the day. Some people fall asleep within minutes of hitting the pillow; others devise elaborate rituals before retiring - exercising, brushing their teeth, drinking a glass of water, reading a bit of a favorite novel.

A microwave oven, sensing the vapor rising from the turkey inside, decides the bird is done and automatically lowers the temperature setting to warm. A dishwasher waits until midnight to start its wash cycle, taking advantage of off-peak electrical rates. A coffee maker stirs into action 10 minutes before its owner awakes, automatically grinding and brewing the morning coffee. Microprocessors are infiltrating kitchen appliances - monitoring their performance, regulating their temperature and timing, and diagnosing their malfunctions.

The Bath Womb is much more than a bathtub - it is therapy, a retreat, a form of escapist bathing. It is one of the wonders that are raising the bath in today's high-tech house to the height of importance that it enjoyed in ancient Rome. The trends in the bathroom reflect the widening consumer interest in electronic aids to better health.

New arrangements and relationships among and between elements of the erstwhile Bell System that took effect on Jan. 1, 1984, will have ramifications to the end of the century at least. AT&T's defense against the breakup had gone on for so long that lawyers involved in the case were thought to have lifetime assignments. The case history will provide decades' worth of fodder for business schools.

articleTitle: Paul E. Green Jr. on communications: Progress in fiber optics, LANs, and PBXs
abstract: In the wake of the Bell System divestiture, Bell's operating companies, AT&T Long Lines, and the product offerings of the former system have gone their separate ways. The effects of the divestiture on technological innovation are not yet known, but the divestiture was the big communications event of 1984.

You come home from a contentious day at work. You're tense, and a big lunch has left you slightly dyspeptic; some instant exercise and a massage might release that tension and improve your metabolism. With microprocessors and sensors converting professional physical fitness equipment into consumer items, it's possible to turn a room in your home into a miniature health club [Fig. 1].

articleTitle: Spectral lines: 'The challenge of all time'
abstract: Lest anyone suppose that there is a holistic logic to the concept of the Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI), rest assured that there is not. That is because the scenarios, time frames, weapons, and even the "players" are still unknown or ill-defined. The best that can be said is that, in the minds of many of the most informed scholars of military strategy, the United States has no better alternative. The investment in the SDI is a necessity, they believe.

articleTitle: The experts' outlook: Eric M. Aupperle on computers: Networking is key to future growth
abstract: The communications and computer industries evolved independently, but they have blended inexorably, both technically and, more recently, organizationally. This trend will surely continue as local, regional, national, and international networks develop and expand their links.

I live in a low-tech home. Nothing in my home beeps, buzzes, radiates, programs, or reads out digitally. No, I do not live in a cave. Nor am I a technophobe. Professionally, I work with multimillion-dollar television electronics. But when I go home, I do not want to depend on more than a push-button blender for my comfort and leisure.

articleTitle: Software: Artificial-intelligence software becomes available for minis and mainframes, and the U.S. Department of Defense converts to Ada and pushes to produce secure systems
abstract: Major mainframe and minicomputer manufacturers entered the artificial-intelligence software field in 1984. IBM introduced a version of the LISP artificial-intelligence programming language for its 370 family of mainframe computers, and Digital Equipment Corp. and Data General Corp. of Westboro, Mass., also introduced versions of LISP for their minicomputers. DEC's VAX LISP and Data General's Common LISP are both implementations of the Common LISP standard dialect of the language, for which specification was worked out over the past several years by AI researchers. Both the AI programming languages and the AI programming environments introduced last year are tools for building applications programs; widescale use of AI techniques is still in the future.

articleTitle: Instrumentation: Bench instruments are linked by personal computers and the steps in devising chip tests and designing chips are linked by software
abstract: Personal computers strengthened their foothold in the instrumentation field last year. New programs to acquire and analyze data became available for applications ranging from repairing computers to controlling manufacturing instruments.

articleTitle: Transportation: New computer controls make travel more comfortable, thyristors cut costs of motor operation, and new steering systems for cars are tested to improve fuel economy
abstract: Trains operating on the Bay Area Rapid Transit (BART) system in San Francisco will soon get “a new and very special passenger - the microprocessor,- reported” David Turner, an electronics specialist with Booz Allen & Hamilton Inc., a consulting firm in Los Angeles, Calif. “What makes this passenger so special,“ he wrote in the May 1984 issue of a newsletter put out by the IEEE Vehicular Technology Society, “is that it will be in full control of the sleek, 80-mile-per-hour trains.”

articleTitle: Spectral lines: Where are our heroes?
abstract: Recently U.S. News & World Report conducted a poll of young adults in the United States, asking them: “Who are your heroes or heroines “ that is, what public figures living anywhere in the world do you find personally inspiring and would you hope to be like in some way?” Years ago, such a poll might have yielded names like Thomas Edison, Alexander Graham Bell, or Thomas Watson, but this one did not - at least, not in the top 10. Clint Eastwood was No. 1, and actor-comedian Eddie Murphy No. 2.

What is the purpose of the MX missile? How does it relate to the Strategic Defense Initiative (“Star Wars”)? How will it lead to a ban on all nuclear weapons? At the height of the President's campaign in March to force a favorable vote on the MX by Congress, a group of national magazine editors and publishers were invited to a White House briefing for the purpose - at least in part - of hearing the Administration's views on these questions. President Reagan and his chief of staff, Donald Regan, addressed the invited group on a variety of topics, including the MX and the defense budget.

Lighting for the high-tech home is more than just screwing incandescent bulbs into ceiling fixtures and arranging floor lamps, desk lamps, and night lights. Instead, designed lighting - the creation of different moods by changing the intensity, focus, and color of lights - is becoming more and more widespread as people see what a difference it can make to their environment, explained John Kaufman, technical director of the Illuminating Engineering Society in New York.

articleTitle: Hello again the future of telecommunications

abstract: Most of you read Spectrum to learn more about some technical specialty other than your own. That's the reason most often given in answer to the reader survey that appeared in the September issue. The second most frequently cited reason was to learn more about your own specialty. A few readers pointed out that when they're reading about someone else's specialty, Spectrum sometimes treats it a bit more deeply than they require, whereas when they're reading about their own, they'd often like more detail than we provide. Perhaps, mused one, this means that all articles are just about right.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: Just for the fun of it
abstract: There ought to be some fun to every occupation - whether it be night-desk clerking or posting accounts. Our own profession should be brimming with opportunities for enjoyment. Didn't we follow it because it offered unlimited challenges to be creative, innovative, inventive - solving problems for the benefit of ourselves, our organizations, and sometimes even humanity?

articleTitle: Eaglecrest: A commuter's dream: Communication is everything in this high-tech aerie in the foothills of the Sierra Nevada; it is designed to permit the professional to work at home, far from the madding crowd
abstract: The emergence of the information age is changing the way homes are built. Just as today's home builder installs adequate power, water, and sewage lines, the builder of the future is expected to furnish adequate data-communications links. At least one home developer has already moved in this direction in Foresthill, Calif.

In the high-tech living room, consumers can spend considerable cash to refine and perfect their audio systems, but does all the latest and most expensive gear make a difference? The answer often is no. In the first place, an audio system is never better than its weakest link. The perfection of a compact disk player is often not matched with correspondingly perfect speakers; audio engineers say the perfect speaker has yet to be built. And beyond the electronics, the most expensive living room system will sound only as good as the acoustics of the room allow.

Among the characteristics of the best-read Spectrum articles are, not surprisingly, the following: they are interesting, informative, instructive, and useful. But beyond that, they tend to answer certain questions: How does it work? How is it used? How much does it cost? How can it fail? How does it hook together? In each case, “it” may refer to materials, components, subsystems, or systems. And each technical article may emphasize certain characteristics: it may be tutorial, applications oriented, systems oriented, or R&D oriented. It may contain a notable element of timeliness, news-worthiness, or controversy.

Personal computers and modems, supplemented by videodisks, are turning the study in the home into a chameleon-like room that can, as the occasion demands, become a working office, a stockbroker's wire room, a classroom, a library, or a relaxing den. The study itself need not be confined to any one particular section of the high-tech house but can be “created” on the spot, wherever the computer system or videodisk player happens to be found in the home.

If precollege students are uneducated in mathematics and science, there's a high probability they'll not consider careers in engineering. Many superior minds may thus be lost to the field of engineering.

Personal computers and computer-based systems are turning two of the oldest hobbies in the United States - amateur radio and model railroading - into high-tech pastimes. Many modern hams no longer spin a high-frequency radio dial at random while transmitting “Calling CQ, calling CQ” they track satellites with a personal computer and swap software over the air. The model railroader with a big layout need no longer activate each track signal or switch by hand; when a computer is coupled to the tracks, it can help control the lines.

articleTitle: Bernard T. Murphy on solid state: Biopolar and MOS on the same chip?
abstract: The rapid evolution of silicon technology has already created two revolutions and more lie ahead. This year marks the twenty-fifth anniversary of the introduction of Fairchild's RTL family, which were the first integrated circuits to have all circuit elements defined photolithographically on the same chip. About 1970, integrated circuits evolved into the system on a chip. What's to come?

articleTitle: What's ahead: Choices for tomorrow: Sobering institutional and technical issues will determine the shape of future telecommunications systems
abstract: What will the postdivestiture telecommunications industry look like over the next 5 to 15 years? That picture will be determined not only by the emergence of new technologies but also by judicial, regulatory, and legislative decisions that will shape the industry in the United States and other countries. Some trends can be extrapolated into clear scenarios; others are more contradictory - primarily because there is now a major new element in the business: stiff competition and its concomitant risk.

Television commercials to the contrary, it is doubtful that anyone actually waxes ecstatic over doing the laundry. However, microprocessors, sensors, and new controls in washers and dryers have reduced the drudgery to a minimum. The machines are even smart enough to adjust to the individual load without requiring someone to check on the progress of the wash.

articleTitle: Spectral Lines: Education: Good news and bad
abstract: In response to “crisis” labels that had been attached to engineering education in the United States five or six years ago, the National Research Council undertook a study lasting some two years. Its report was released in May 1985. Entitled “Engineering Education and Practice in the United States,” it dealt with undergraduate education, graduate education and research, continuing education, and utilization of engineers.

To a question posed by a news reporter during the presidential debate on Oct. 21, 1984, about whether to “share the best of America's technology in this weapons area with our principal adversary,” President Reagan replied, “Why not? I hope we can.” He was referring to the sophisticated technology for an unnamed defensive weapon to “reduce the utility” of nuclear arms, as he had phrased it during a press conference earlier in the year.

articleTitle: John J. Dougherty on power and energy: How much power from what sources?
abstract: Electric utilities are faced with two major interrelated problems: How much additional power will be needed between now and the turn of the century? And how will it be generated? Nearly all other problems can be considered subsets of these two issues.

When 32-bit microprocessor chips were introduced for workstations a few years ago, there was some talk of using them ultimately in personal computers - but it was hard to imagine what a single PC user would do with all that processing power. Today software developers are introducing some products that strain the available memory and processing speed of 16-bit high-end personal computers in anticipation of upgrades.

articleTitle: Consumer electronics: Stereo sound for television and new video technologies grabbed and held the consumer-electronics spotlight in 1984
abstract: Growth in color-television sales was slowing. The video-game industry had matured much faster than expected and appeared to be rapidly deteriorating. Prototypes of high-definition television sets and direct-broadcast-satellite receivers had been demonstrated, but some industry officials predicted that it would be another year at least until those technologies turned up in products. Digital video and audio disks were no longer news and were not selling as well as had been expected. And teletext and videotex ventures were folding. In short, the consumer-electronics industry appeared to be entering a period of hibernation in January 1984 [Fig. 1].

articleTitle: Aerospace and military: Three satellites are salvaged in space, an Army intercept missile destroys a mock ICBM warhead, and a new strategic bomber that's harder to detect is unveiled
abstract: The Minuteman I intercontinental ballistic missile hurtled into space from Vandenberg Air Force Base in southern California on June 10, 1984. About 25 minutes later an optically guided missile was launched from the Kwajalein test range in the Pacific, some 7800 kilometers (4200 nautical miles) away. The guided missile's mission: to intercept the ICBM's dummy warhead.

Can you envision a house with 20 television monitors, 13 personal computers, a host of control, communications, and security systems, and its own local area network? How about a house that gets its heat from 400 feet below the ground, has walls and floors that store radiant heat during the day and release it at night, with windows that allow more heat to enter than escape? Such houses exist; you can read about them in this issue of Spectrum.

articleTitle: Tactile sensors and the gripping challenge: Increasing the performance of sensors over a wide range of force is a first step toward robotry that can hold and manipulate objects as humans do
abstract: Even a blindfolded human can tell the difference between a hammer and an egg and handle each object accordingly. But how do you instruct a robot to recognize the difference and to apply just enough pressure in handling to keep the egg from cracking or the hammer from slipping to the ground?

articleTitle: Power devices are in the chips: New power integrated circuits, called PICs, put both power-handling semiconductors and logic on the same IC chip; soon they may be part of every household appliance
abstract: Today's automobile is burdened with some 100 pounds of wiring. It could be cut to 50. Commercial airliners carry some 8000 lb of electric wiring. It could be cut to a few hundred pounds. Standard power integrated circuits could help do the job, if only they were available. Power integrated circuits would help utilities and their rate-payers as well; ac motors consume more than 50 percent of all the electricity used in the United States, much of which is wasted because the motors run at constant speed. Variable-speed motors in washing machines, air conditioners, and machine tools - under the control of power ICs - would eliminate this vast waste.

articleTitle: Probing beneath the sea: Sending vessels into environments too harsh for humans poses challenges in communications, artificial intelligence, and power-supply technology
abstract: When a U.S Air Force B-52 bomber collided in midair with its refueling plane near Palomares, Spain, in 1966, a 20-megaton hydrogen bomb was released that wafted harmlessly under a parachute until it sank 870 meters deep in the Mediterranean Sea. For obvious reasons of national security and international politics, the U.S. Navy moved quickly to locate the undetonated bomb. It spliced some 300 meters of extra cable onto the tether of a submersible called the Cable Controlled Underwater Recovery Vehicle: an unmanned vehicle equipped with a television camera, a manipulator arm, and a control tether that attached the vehicle to a support ship. With the help of the unmanned submersible, the Navy salvaged the bomb within three months.

articleTitle: Research at xerox PARC: A founder's assessment: The first director of the Xerox Palo Alto Research Center tells how his management philosophy worked in launching the center and making it a success
abstract: Suppose you had the chance to set up and manage a research center for a large office-equipment corporation. How would you go about it? What fundamentals would guide you in directing the researchers to create systems and products that would be ahead of the competition, if not ahead of their time?

articleTitle: Laser diodes are power-packed: Single-mode laser diodes have a rosy future, both as individual sources of power up to 100 milliwatts and in arrays promising up to half a watt
abstract: They are individually no bigger than a grain of table salt and require but 100 to 200 milliwatts of electric power to operate, but semiconductor diode lasers are viewed as ideal light sources. First demonstrated as being feasible in the pulsed mode in 1962 and used in low-power continuous-wave applications since the late 1970s, they are now poised for what researchers hope will be a great leap to a multitude of high-power applications.

articleTitle: Power-line fields and human health: Can exposure to 60-Hz fields cause biological problems in humans? The answer may be found through a process of risk assessment
abstract: Can human exposure to power-frequency electromagnetic fields have significant health consequences? Few people would have given this question a second thought 30 or 40 years ago, when electricity was considered the clean, safe marvel of the modern world. Today, however, the question of exposure to power-frequency fields is the subject of serious scientific study and heated public debate.

articleTitle: Gutting chip-testing costs: Designing VLSI circuits for testability is the most efficient way to reduce the relative costs of assuring high chip reliability
abstract: Most engineers would agree that the quality of an integrated circuit depends partly on the ability to test it. But many chips now hold over 10 000 devices, and the cost of testing tends to increase in proportion to the square of the number of devices on the chip. The problem of containing testing costs while ensuring chip quality is one that all semiconductor manufacturers face.

Creative people often leave their companies when they fed frustrated in their attempts to implement ideas. If their parent companies had empowered them with the freedom to run their own small business within the company, chances are that many would not have left. Now a few corporations are realizing that innovation comes more easily to small organizations and are beginning to foster their own intracompany entrepreneurs - or “intrapreneurs.”

articleTitle: Toward simpler, faster computers: By omitting unnecessary functions, designers of reduced-instruction-set computers increase system speed and hold down equipment costs
abstract: An overriding direction taken by computer design over the last 30 years - packing more and more functions into computing hardware to handle more complex problems - is being challenged as self-defeating.

articleTitle: More than mainframes: Power utilities are finding that the mix-and-match trend that is evident in computer systems is for them a matter of survival
abstract: A mix-and-match trend is taking hold in computer systems design. Rather than relying on one mainframe or minicomputer to do all their computing tasks, more and more industries are blending microcomputers, minicomputers, and mainframes to take advantage of the best features of each. When properly assembled, such a system excels not only in manipulating numbers in large and lengthy calculations, a job traditionally done with mainframes; but it also can simultaneously and repeatedly process simple data in real time, work best handled by mini- and microcomputers.

The pioneers of the Xerox Palo Alto Research Center, founded in 1970, worked to create the “office of the future.” The results of their efforts have found their way into innovative products from many companies, including Xerox Corp. itself.

In 1931 Edwin A. Link marketed the Link Trainer, his first aircraft flight simulator, as a coin-operated amusement device. He traveled the county-fair circuit to drum up business, because few people had money to learn to fly. In February 1934, however, after repeated attempts, he finally convinced the Army Air Corps to buy six simulators on a trial basis. He met with such immediate success that over 10 000 simulators were produced by the end of World War II by Link Aviation Inc., and more than half a million Allied pilots were trained with them during that time.

Fault-tolerant computers have caught up with the microprocessor revolution. A new approach to fault-tolerant computer design - systems based on multiple microprocessors - is winning followers and challenging the decade-old approach that relies on central processing units (CPUs) made up of medium- and large-scale integrated circuits. Like their predecessors, the multiple microprocessor systems trade throughput for reliability and are proving invaluable in financial transactions, telephony, and a number of other applications that demand high reliability.

articleTitle: Pulsed power packs a punch: Lasers, electromagnetic launchers, and fusion reactors require enormous, instantaneous pulses of power not available from the utilities' mains
abstract: Electric power is routinely supplied by utilities in a continuous flow. But for many applications, ranging from thermonuclear-fusion research and high-energy particle accelerators to lasers and electromagnetic launchers, power must be delivered in short, huge bursts. To deliver this “pulsed” power, energy must be collected at low power, stored, and then released almost instantaneously.

articleTitle: Taming EMI in microprocessor systems: The authors propose a systematic approach to limiting the effects of electromagnetic interference
abstract: It was late one summer afternoon in 1983, near the end of the day shift at a steel plant in the eastern United States. An operator using a new radio link was guiding the last ladle of molten steel as it moved along an overhead track from the blast furnace to the ingot molds. Soon the end-of-shift horn would sound. Without warning, the ladle tipped prematurely as it neared the molds, pouring hot steel on the floor and on some of the workers.

articleTitle: Robots do the dirty work: Some walk, some roll as they go about their tedious, hazardous chores in nuclear-power plants
abstract: We've seen it on the evening news: a robot enters a building suspected of containing a bomb. The police steer the robot remotely, watching a television screen that shows what the robot “sees.” The robot picks up the suitcase on command with its mechanical arm, then rolls out of the building and drops the suitcase into a concrete tumbler to protect the bomb squad in case it explodes.

articleTitle: Automating the power grid: Real-time communication between customers, the electricity grid, and power plants can cut costs for both supplier and user; the technology options are many
abstract: In the ideal world, computers at utilities would directly monitor electricity use by each consumer. Many studies have demonstrated that power utilities can save money through real-time monitoring and control of all points along their distribution systems. But a real-time system requires communication between thousands of units in the field and a central computer, where the intelligence is available to process the data and transmit control commands. And it is here that utilities have come a cropper.

articleTitle: Fiber optics: Poised to displace satellites: Expansion of fiber-optic cable networks will lead to the creation of new communication services and may limit the role of satellites
abstract: A tremendous expansion of fiber-optic cable networks is planned in the telecommunications industry over the next several years, and some specialists are predicting a tidal-wave effect that will buffet the satellite industry and limit its role. At the same time the trend is expected to create new communication services.

articleTitle: Japan reaches beyond silicon: Intent on dominating high-speed computing and optical communications, Japanese laboratories are aggressively studying materials in the gallium arsenide family
abstract: Japanese researchers, convinced that a new solid-state technology is needed to accommodate high-speed computing, optical communications, and other special purposes, are urgently exploring the development of nonsilicon semiconductors. Both the Japanese government and the electronics industry are committed to research into semiconductors made from elements in groups III and V of the periodic table. The ultimate goal: to dominate the world market in semiconductors made from compounds such as gallium arsenide - a market that the Japanese estimate will exceed $50 billion by the turn of the century.

articleTitle: The secret six-month project: Why Texas Instruments decided to put the first transistor radio on the market by Christmas 1954 and how it was accomplished
abstract: On a steamy day shortly before the July 4 weekend in 1954, Richard Koch and his boss, Raymond Morris, boarded an American Airlines flight from Chicago to Houston, Texas. Morris, who was chief engineer at an Indianapolis, Ind., electronics manufacturer called IDEA (Industrial Development Engineering Associates), had told Koch they were simply going to change some parts in UHF converters stocked at IDEA's Texas distributors. But soon after takeoff, Morris settled back and revealed the main purpose of their trip. After stopping in Houston, they would meet with Texas Instruments (TI) engineers in Dallas to begin manufacturing an all-transistor, shirt-pocket radio. This would be the first commercial transistor radio, and at a time when one could buy a table model vacuum-tube radio for $15, it would sell for $49.95.

articleTitle: Lasers cut a swath in surgical and medical applications: Their early promise is being fulfilled, particularly for the surgeon, while research hints at usefulness in nonsurgical cancer therapy
abstract: In the operating room of the not-too-distant future, integrated systems could guide the laser beam during surgery, using digital data from such diagnostic instrumentation as computerized tomography, ultrasound, and nuclear magnetic resonance imaging. Work is now under way to develop such integrated systems. They would help minimize the invasiveness and trauma of surgery, causing much less suffering for the patient than conventional surgical techniques. In addition, they could decrease the costs of medical care by lowering postoperative complications and shortening hospital stays.

articleTitle: Victorian experiments and optical communications: Precursors of fiber-optic communications were invented a century ago, but no one at that time attempted to synthesize the fragmented knowledge
abstract: Sometimes ideas emerge long before their time and then lie dormant for many years until other developments make it possible to put the pieces together for a technological breakthrough - such as fiber-optic communications. Key elements of the concept of communicating via light were known in the late 1800s. Several Victorianera engineers and physicists found ways to guide light through transparent media, distribute light throughout buildings, transmit voices over beams of light, and make fine glass fibers. Yet most were striving for applications largely unrelated to optical communications, and nearly a century would elapse before their ways of manipulating light would be synthesized in the form of fiber-optic communications.

articleTitle: Thwarting the information thieves: Fear of spying through simple or sophisticated electronics has spawned an industry whose challenge is to block the illegal interception of intelligence
abstract: The building was dark, the employees gone for the day. when a team of experts trained in electronic surveillance entered. They went to work quickly. In an office in the heart of the building, one of the experts unscrewed a power-outlet plate and placed a small radio transmitter inside the cavity. Another lifted the plastic casing off the office's telephone; with a screwdriver and needle-nose pliers he altered the circuitry of the telephone so someone tapping the line could listen to conversations in the room as well as on the telephone line. Meanwhile, a third team member was down the hall in the building's telephone room, attaching a small inductive tap to the wire pair leading to the office.

articleTitle: Computers in power: A welcome invader: Supervisory computer systems cut utility costs by scheduling generating units, planning against outages, and coordinating the sale of power
abstract: It's Super Bowl Sunday. Shortly before the championship football game begins, millions of viewers turn on their television sets. On any other Sunday, they might be reading, shopping, or traveling. But today they are all home. Refrigerator doors open, heaters click on, and stoves are lit. The demand for electricity surges.

articleTitle: An American in Tokyo: Jumping to the Japanese beat: During a year's internship, an engineer from Westinghouse learns to move in sync with the hard-driving members of the Mitsubishi team
abstract: The production line at one Westinghouse Electric Corp. factory has a sharp bend in it because of the uneven foundation of the building. When Japan's Mitsubishi Electric Corp., decades ago, took a license for the factory design, it modeled its entire operation after the Westinghouse factory - right down to the crook in the production line. Since 1923, when a licensing agreement between the two was struck, the companies have enjoyed a mirror-close relationship that survived even World War II. During the war Mitsubishi kept track of the royalties it owed Westinghouse and later paid up in stock shares. Westinghouse today owns about 2 percent of Mitsubishi.

articleTitle: The X-29: is it coming or going?
abstract: It is a weird-looking aircraft, with the wing swept forward instead of back, and it may be the most unstable modern jet yet built. Designed to fly and maneuver at transonic speeds - equal or close to the speed of sound - the experimental aircraft relies on a highly complex system of digital computers to assist the pilot.

articleTitle: Mind-boggling complexity: The challenge is to design an intelligent system that finds and destroys targets in a nuclear battlefield
abstract: In a simulation exercise Like the one done by researcher Christopher T. Cunningham at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, it seems almost easy. A salvo of 1400 intercontinental ballistic missiles is fired on the screen, confronting a strategic defense system. Ninety percent of the missiles are picked off by laser battle stations in the boost phase, before they deploy their warheads and penetration aids. The second defensive tier destroys 90 percent of the remaining 10 percent of the missiles; the third and final tier is 90 percent effective against the rest of those that leak through. Overall effectiveness of the system: 99.9 percent.

In January 1981, a handful of semiconductor engineers at MOS Technology in West Chester, Pa., a subsidiary of Commodore International Ltd., began designing a graphics chip and a sound chip to sell to whoever wanted to make “the world's best video game.” In January 1982, a home computer incorporating those chips was introduced at the Winter Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas, Nev. By using in-house integrated-circuit-fabrication facilities for prototyping, the engineers had cut the design time for each chip to less than nine months, and they had designed and built five prototype computers for the show in less than five weeks. What surprised the rest of the home-computer industry most, however, was the introductory price of the Commodore 64: $595 for a unit incorporating a keyboard, a central processor, the graphics and sound chips, and 64 kilobytes of memory instead of the 16 or 32 that were then considered the norm.

articleTitle: Realism in synthetic speech: Synthesized speech may be intelligible, but it often sounds artificial; researchers are solving that problem
abstract: A technician at the Westinghouse Electric Corp.'s defense electronics manufacturing plant in Baltimore peers into a microscope, examining a partially completed hybrid circuit on a wafer.

articleTitle: Superfine IC geometries: Gas-plasma etching may supplant chemical etching in manufacturing high-performance integrated circuits
abstract: To a microlithographer who prepares patterns of integrated circuits on semiconductor materials, a design as narrow as a 100-micrometer-wide human hair would be simply too bulky to be of practical use. The semiconductor industry routinely produces patterns with features much smaller than these, and these patterns are made in large quantities to exacting specifications. A hundred or more production steps must be performed on a thin slice of silicon before the IC chip is finished and can go into a growing line of products. One of these steps is etching, and here the focus of attention among semiconductor vendors is shifting to dry etching.

articleTitle: The friendly fields of RF: Encouraged by successes in fusing fractured bones, researchers look to electromagnetic fields for healing wounds and shrinking tumors
abstract: Radio-frequency radiation in medicine - widely used to help heal bone fractures - is also showing promise for healing flesh wounds, regenerating nerves, and treating advanced cancers.

articleTitle: The superstructure: Designing for high-tech: The high-tech house is hardly passive; its heating, security, communications, and lighting systems function independently, yet talk with one another at the command of computers
abstract: When John Holder goes away for a winter weekend, he doesn't ask a neighbor to take care of his house in Midland, Mich. The house takes care of itself. If someone should break into his home on Friday evening, a booming synthesized voice will confront the burglar, telling him that he has been detected and that the police, automatically summoned, are on their way.

articleTitle: Exotic weaponry: Lasers, particle beams, and high-speed projectiles are expected to be the backbone of the SDI arsenal
abstract: As enemy intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs) rise from their silos and submarines, an array of defensive weapons are alerted. The large, slow-burning ICBM boosters fall victim to the homing warheads launched from space-based rocket pods. Fast-burning boosters are impinged by lasers from other space platforms or from the ground. The same suite of weapons, along with space-based particle beams, engage postboost vehicles as they dispense warheads and decoys.

articleTitle: The beauty of 32 bits: This near-optimum bit width has unprecedented potential for the well-informed designer of microprocessor-based systems
abstract: Rarely has an advancement in microelectronics been so long awaited and so loudly trumpeted as the introduction of the 32-bit microprocessor. Not long after the first 4- and 8-bit microprocessors were introduced in the early 1970s and 16-bit chips were on the horizon, designers realized that the progression would eventually lead to microprocessors that accessed and manipulated addresses and data 32 bits at a time. General-purpose minicomputers and mainframes had more or less already settled on that bit width as a good compromise between speed, which favors long bit widths for faster access to large blocks of data, and efficiency, which limits the width to avoid wasting bits.

articleTitle: Perfecting the picture: A guide is offered for handicapping the race for first place in flat-panel displays; none can yet match CRTs for price and performance
abstract: In a typical portable computer the electronic circuits are elegantly packaged on a few chips; the bulk comes from the cathode-ray tube - which requires considerable depth - that displays the computer's work. Now three new technologies are creating flat-panel displays that potentially will reduce the computer to a truly kneetop package.

articleTitle: From data to image to action: Manipulating digital images created from raw data proves to be a potent tool in human decision making
abstract: Humans do image analysis constantly and mostly without conscious effort. From the millions of bits of data in the photo receptors of the retinas, the eyes extract pictorial, numerical, and other information while the mind filters out only information that is relevant.

articleTitle: Looking ahead with confidence: Cases of technological forecasts that failed are well known, yet careful use of forecasting techniques can help avoid misdirected R&D
abstract: In the late 1940s and early 1950s many experts predicted that nuclear-generated electricity would be much cheaper than fossil-fueled power, and even as late as a decade ago the consensus prediction was for a rapid growth in nuclear generation in the United States. Today nuclear power is on the ropes.

articleTitle: The innovation revolution awaits: Expectations of a technological bonanza might have been inflated, but new openings are seen for the entrepreneurial opportunist
abstract: One of the bonuses of breaking up the Bell System, proponents of divestiture argued in the early 1980s, would be a plethora of new technologies. With fierce competition, this line of reasoning went, the success of AT&T and its competitors would depend on ability to introduce useful new technologies. As the first year of divestiture drew to a close, a Business Week headline asked: “Did it make sense to break up AT&T?”

articleTitle: Videotex: Return engagement: Undaunted by unsuccessful ventures, U.S. corporate giants are planning new investments to give the technology a second chance
abstract: It all seemed so promising a decade ago. The Age of Information had arrived, and a new technology “ videotex ” would bring the power of remote computers into the living rooms of millions. Using cheap terminals and local phone lines, videotex customers could call up thousands of pages of news, sports, travel schedules, and other colorfully illustrated information, as well as on-line shopping and home banking.

articleTitle: HVDC: Wheeling lots of power: Moving power from where it is plentiful to where it is needed may be more efficient than building oil-fired or nuclear plants locally
abstract: It has been 31 years since the first commercial high-voltage, direct-current transmission line was built, but only today are HVDC lines coming into their own. Why the surge of interest in a technology that has been applied on a relatively limited scale for so long? The answer has as much to do with disenchantment with oil-fired and nuclear power plants as with the virtues of HVDC.

articleTitle: Debating the issues: The greatest challenge of all may be gaining political support for the SDI both in the U.S. and elsewhere
abstract: The Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI) poses staggering challenges to engineers and scientists. But political issues - not technical ones - may loom even larger as obstacles to the program's progress.

articleTitle: From lab to lap: Liquid-crystal, electroluminescent, and plasma displays are among the major contenders for use in truly portable computers
abstract: Computers are habit-forming; at home and in the office they draft reports, tally figures, query information services, and order airline tickets. But as the habit grows, access to computers in the home and office is no longer enough. Today's computer users want to be able to draft memos while airborne on route to a meeting, to dial into the office computer from a phone booth and collect the latest data, and to access Dow Jones' stock and bond information with a pocket-size radio terminal. In short, they need a computer to take along with them wherever they go.

articleTitle: Fiber-optic system tradeoffs: With the choice of short-wavelength and long-wavelength technologies available, the designer can tailor a fiber-optic system to specific applications
abstract: A wide choice of components for fiber-optic systems are now available: transmitters, fibers, and receivers for operation at short wavelengths (less than 1 micrometer) or long wavelengths (more than 1 micrometer). Each of these components has its own advantages and disadvantages and its own set of tradeoffs in any particular application. But the very existence of such choices means that the best system for any given application can now be assembled.

articleTitle: Chip pirates: Beware the law: A new Federal statute is written to protect semiconductor chip designs; the law, however, contains ambiguities that have yet to be tested
abstract: In 1982 Intersil Inc., a California-based subsidiary of General Electric Co., sued Teledyne Semiconductor for copying analog-type semiconductor chips. Intersil felt that the copying was an infringement under copyright law; however, Teledyne countered that its actions were not illegal since it is not possible to copyright a useful article. Meanwhile, since the late 1970s Intel Corp. had disputes with at least three Japanese companies that had made close copies of its 8086 16-bit microprocessor chip. And Mostek Corp.'s 16-K MK4116 memory chip was copied by no fewer than 15 different companies.

articleTitle: Safeguarding the national security: Can the military and other Government functions be confident that the newly fragmented telecommunications system will respond to crises?
abstract: Ten years ago, before the American Telephone & Telegraph Co. installed a new long-distance system, it asked the U.S. Department of Defense what route it should take. Defense officials looked over their highly classified “laydown” maps, showing the expected targets of a Soviet nuclear strike, and told AT&T which route was most survivable - that is, which was farthest from targets. The company then used that path, folding any extra cost into its rate base.

articleTitle: Power and energy: Utilities boost efficiency and save money through energy-management systems, pumped storage, and fuel cells, while industrial producers pursue cogeneration
abstract: It has been the theme of the 1980s so far in the United States: utilities have not added nearly as much generating capacity as they had planned. In the 1960s and 1970s, demand for electricity grew at 7 percent per year, but in 1979 electricity consumption began to recede. The North American Electric Reliability Council, an industry group in Princeton, N.J., predicts total annual growth of but 2.7 percent through 1993. Rather than building new units, utilities are now concentrating on improving their efficiency and lowering their costs for power generation, transmission, and distribution.

articleTitle: Medical electronics: NMR reaches the marketplace, biosensors show promise, and progress is made in pacemakers and implantable drug pumps
abstract: Medical interest in the human heart intensified last year, and electronic equipment makers, pressing to keep up, reported new developments in at least five areas. Advances in cardiac imaging occurred in computed tomography, ultrasound, and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR). Pacemakers and heartassist systems also progressed.

articleTitle: The telecommunications bazaar: Suppliers of telecommunications equipment and services find opportunities but crowded markets in everything from telephones to toll switches
abstract: A word used quite frequently by telecommunications systems market analysts these days is “chaos”

Instruments that can "see" the atom are becoming essential to fabricate and diagnose electron devices , integrated circuits as well as discrete devices. Such resolution was unheard of only a few years ago. But the growth of thin films by vapor deposition, patterning by electron-beam lithography, and doping by low-energy ion implantation have opened the way to microelectronics on an incredibly fine scale. As a result, new devices like the modulation-doped field-effect transistor (MODFET) now control the transport of electrons through layers only a few atoms thick.
When AT&T and the U.S. Justice Department agreed to break up the Bell System, one of the questions most often raised was: What will happen to Bell Labs?

articleTitle: Solid state: In smarter design and fabrication of ICs, power and logic are mixed on the same chip and circuits are integrated over an entire wafer
abstract: After several years of concentrated effort to make integrated-circuit features even smaller, solid-state engineers turned last year to new approaches that heighten the level of circuit integration, thus decreasing the cost and improving the reliability of systems by eliminating wiring and reducing the number of components. On the IC level, designers began to place logic gates and power-control devices on the same chip instead of building separate chips and wiring them together.

articleTitle: The decision to divest: Incredible or inevitable? The contest that ultimately fractured the Bell System was as much a clash between the participants' deeply held philosophies as it was about antitrust laws
abstract: The telephone was ringing in a condominium of the Park City, Utah, Ski Lodge on the evening of Jan. 2, 1982, as Assistant Attorney General William F. Baxter was walking in after his first day on the snowy mountain slopes. The voice on the other end of the line was that of Charles L. Brown, chairman of the board of AT&T, calling from Florida.

articleTitle: The consumer reels in the aftermath: Changing rules, rising rates, questionable quality, and overwhelming options challenge the residential subscriber
abstract: Many consumers think the breakup of the Bell System was a bad idea. They point to a mound of supporting evidence:

It wasn't exactly a dignified job that the president of the Digital Equipment Corp. had taken on, but there he was, with a group of students employed temporarily by Digital, carting away a mountain of rubbish outside a small software company in West Concord, Mass. Finally the executive, Kenneth Olsen, had found what he was looking for that summer in 1973: that rubbish was the disassembled remains of an early computer, the Whirlwind.

articleTitle: Weathering the storm: Terminations and transfers: Uncertainty became the dominant theme on Jan. 1, 1984 for employees of both AT&T and the Bell operating companies
abstract: Life on the job is looking pretty good for George Maeda these days. Ever since the divestiture of the Bell operating companies, his work for AT&T Bell Laboratories on fiber-optic systems with high bit rates has proceeded at an invigorating clip. 6370699The pace of product development,” he said, “has gone through the ceiling.” So has the number of phone calls Maeda and his colleagues have received from job head-hunters interested in their talents.

articleTitle: Less sizzle, more beef for Detroit in '86: Increasing electronic content in 1986 models represents serious functions like transmission, engine, and antitheft controls, antilock braking, and diagnostics
abstract: More guts and gumption and less glitz and glitter is the trend in 1986 models from the Big Three car makers in the United States. There are still a few overdone electronic dashboards and unnecessary driver “aids,” but for the most part electronic devices and systems have been applied functionally to add true value for car buyers.

articleTitle: Portia's perfect pad: Superhigh-tech: It may be too high-tech for some tastes, but an IEEE-member husband-and-wife team waits eagerly to move into this state-of-the-art Dallas showplace
abstract: “The house will contain 10 IBM computers on a local area network, an Apple He, and two Apple Macintoshes. You can never have too many computers.”

articleTitle: The workhorse CRT: New life: This old standby is still first in monochrome text displays, and color CRTs are widely chosen for graphics
abstract: After playing key roles in the television, electronic-instrument, and computer fields for four decades, the cathode-ray-tube display is still being improved. New developments in both color and monochrome monitors for computers are yielding higher contrast, better resolution, and more subtle shading.

articleTitle: Invasions and counterinvasions: Tariffs, protectionism, and politics affect the struggle for pieces of the huge international telecommunications pie
abstract: The United States is not alone in undergoing drastic change in its telecommunications network. Telecommunications in some non-U.S. countries are also caught in the greatest turmoil in years.

articleTitle: Bypassing is big business for business: Both traditional and unconventional suppliers vie for the corporate dollar
abstract: Twenty-five percent of the large corporations in the United States bypass the local and long-distance telephone systems. They are using a range of techniques and media - including private telecommunication companies, dedicated fiber optics, satellites, and microwaves - to conduct voice and data communications.

articleTitle: VLSI system design by the numbers: Design frames and system kits promise to simplify the development of VLSI-based systems
abstract: New facilities for the rapid design and fabrication of integrated circuits have significantly eased the task of building systems based on custom chips. With such aids as computer-based layout and simulation tools, remote fabrication services - which make chips from designs sent over a computer network - have put custom-chip development within the reach of the application designer, not just the semiconductor engineer.

articleTitle: Planning a probing voyage to Jupiter: The adroit Galileo spacecraft, crammed with advanced instrumentation, should answer some age-old questions about the mysterious planet
abstract: What makes Jupiter's Great Red Spot red? How were planets formed? One of the most complex unmanned explorations of a planet ever undertaken, scheduled to begin next May when a two-in-one spacecraft " one part an orbiter, the other an atmospheric probe " sets out on a four-year mission to explore Jupiter and its four largest satellites, may furnish some answers. The craft Galileo, designed and built by the United States with significant international participation, will be launched from the space shuttle. Its mission will be to return to the Jovian system observed distantly in the 1970s by the Pioneer and Voyager vehicles and to penetrate Jupiter's atmosphere to take samples for the first time.
